soil-agri-082.title: Soil survey: putting an area's soils on the map
soil-agri-082.text: For decades, a US county's soil survey arrived as a printed book, and it could take years to publish. A soil survey, also called soil mapping, classifies the soil types and other soil properties of an area and records where each one lies. It applies soil science and draws heavily on geomorphology, physical geography, patterns of vegetation and land use, and theories of {{ref:soil-form-042}}. Its primary data come from field sampling and from remote sensing, mainly aerial photography. LiDAR and other digital techniques are steadily gaining ground. In the second half of the 20th century, soil mapping meant field survey and drawing soil-type boundaries by hand. Map scales varied by country and purpose. Surveyors carried paper air photos, topographic maps and mapping keys. Many now carry a rugged tablet with GPS, digital imagery, LiDAR and soil geodatabases. In the United States, the program described in {{ref:soil-hist-051}} once published a book for each county. A typical county survey held a general map of soils and a detailed map of indexed soil series. It added a section on soil use and management, and tables of land-use suitability. Today surveys appear on the web, the story of {{ref:soil-agri-170}}, through a service run by the federal agency known as the NRCS, the subject of {{ref:soil-hist-050}}. There users build custom surveys, and changes go live in moments. The agency has maps and data online for more than 95 percent of US counties.

soil-agri-093.title: Matheron's three-part model of soil variation
soil-agri-093.text: Every soil measurement hides three parts. The universal model of soil variation writes a soil variable as Z(s) = m(s) + ε′(s) + ε″. The three parts are a deterministic trend, a spatially autocorrelated random part and leftover noise. Spatially autocorrelated means nearby values are related. French mathematician Georges Matheron introduced the model, and it has proven the best unbiased linear predictor for spatial data. The method of {{ref:soil-meth-004}} uses it to predict or simulate soils; this variant of {{ref:soil-meth-003}} is also called its universal form. The trend is often modeled from the classic soil-forming factors: climate, organisms, relief, parent material and time, the CLORPT model.

soil-bio-008.title: Five hundred sheep beneath a football pitch
soil-bio-008.text: The organisms living beneath a football pitch are estimated to equal the size of 500 sheep. Soil biodiversity is the relationship between soil and that variety of life, including the aspects of soil that can be managed with it in mind. Soil is chiefly a habitat for microbes such as bacteria and fungi. It also houses tiny animals such as protozoa and {{ref:soil-bio-193}}, small ones such as potworms and {{ref:soil-bio-209}}, and larger ones such as earthworms, termites and millipedes. Their primary role is to recycle dead organic material from the plant-based food web above ground. In turn, their activity is a primary factor in how soil forms, physically and chemically. The link shows on maps: natural and farm vegetation boundaries closely follow soil boundaries, even at continental and global scales. Microbial exudates are now accepted as the main force that binds soil particles into clumps and shields carbon from further breakdown. Soil health depends on this diversity. Living covers on the soil and carbon-containing amendments improve it. {{ref:soil-agri-004}}, crop diversification, legume intercrops and organic inputs all correlate with more diverse soil life.

soil-bio-015.title: The microbial loop: how predators free nutrients for roots
soil-bio-015.text: Farooq Azam, Tom Fenchel and others coined the term microbial loop in 1983 for the role of bacteria in marine carbon and nutrient cycles. It names the pathway by which bacteria take up dissolved organic carbon and pass it back up the food web. 'Microbial food web' is now often used instead. In soil, the loop concerns carbon and the nutrients freed when protozoa and {{ref:soil-bio-193}} eat bacteria fed by roots. It runs like this. Roots pushing into new soil prime resting bacteria, which naked amoebae then eat. That frees mineral nitrogen for root hairs to absorb. Predation by amoebae and free-living roundworms raises the rate at which nutrients are released, which in turn stimulates root growth. This loop is Clarholm's hypothesis, and it is hard to verify by experiment. Bacteria-eating protozoa release the nutrients locked in microbial bodies in a form plants can use. A related idea, the model in {{ref:soil-bio-266}}, has plants add carbon through {{ref:soil-bio-142}} and litter. Microbes then either respire it to the atmosphere or store it in a stable pool as dead microbial matter, called necromass. They transform plant carbon outside the cell with enzymes and inside it as their populations grow and die. The balance between pathways that release CO2 and those that build carbon sets how much carbon the soil keeps. Fresh plant carbon can also prime microbes to break down carbon already stored in soil organic matter faster than models expect. Much remains unknown. Most of the soil microbiome has never been cultivated, which leaves its part in carbon cycling uncertain and hampers climate models of carbon flux.

soil-bio-031.title: Funnels, cores and lamps: getting animals out of soil
soil-bio-031.text: Counting soil animals starts with getting them out of the soil. Samples are often taken with a metal core. Large animals such as earthworms can be picked out by hand, but that is impossible for {{ref:soil-bio-193}} and small arthropods. A dry Berlese funnel drives the animals of {{ref:soil-bio-209}} downward, away from light and heat, into a collecting vial. A wet Baermann funnel collects these worms, which sink because they cannot swim. Microbes need other tricks. They are characterized by their respiration, by genetic profiling of extracted cell components, or by biomass estimated before and after fumigation.

soil-bio-056.title: Lithotrophs, the microbes that eat rock
soil-bio-056.text: Life's last universal common ancestor is thought to have been a chemolithotroph, a microbe living on the chemical energy of inorganic substances. A lithotroph is any organism that takes the electrons it needs from an inorganic substance, usually of mineral origin, rather than from organic compounds. It uses them to build cells or make energy. The name joins the Greek lithos, rock, and troph, consumer: lithotrophs are 'eaters of rock'. Lwoff and collaborators suggested the term in 1946. The opposite strategy, covered in {{ref:soil-bio-206}}, gets electrons by breaking down organic compounds. In the broad sense, lithotrophs include light-using photolithotrophs such as plants. Chemolithotrophs, though, are exclusively microorganisms, all in the domains Bacteria and Archaea. Lithoautotrophs take their carbon from carbon dioxide in the air, as plants do. Lithoheterotrophs cannot fix carbon dioxide and must consume organic compounds; only a few bacteria are fully lithoheterotrophic. Many lithotrophs are mixotrophs, topping up the carbon they fix with organic material. They live in the deep subsurface, soils, mines and endolith communities inside rock. There they take part in soil formation and the cycling of carbon, nitrogen and other elements. In the cycling of iron they can use it both ways: as an electron donor, turning Fe(II) into Fe(III), or as an electron acceptor, turning Fe(III) into Fe(II).

soil-bio-075.title: Geosmin, the earthy molecule noses catch in traces
soil-bio-075.text: People can smell geosmin at just 0.006 to 0.01 micrograms per liter of water. Geosmin is a chemical with a distinct earthy or musty smell, made by bacteria common in soil and water. Its name joins the Greek geō-, 'earth', and osmē, 'smell'. Nancy N. Gerber and Hubert A. Lechevalier coined it in 1965 after isolating it from actinomycete cultures, and Gerber worked out its structure in 1968. It is a secondary metabolite, a by-product rather than a necessity of life, of cyanobacteria such as Anabaena, Phormidium and Planktothrix and of actinomycetes, mainly {{ref:soil-bio-225}}. It gives beetroot its earthy taste and contributes to petrichor. The natural (−) form is about eight times more potent than the other, with a mean threshold of 9.5 ng/L against 78 ng/L. With 2-methylisoborneol it is the main biological cause of muddy tastes in drinking water and farmed fish worldwide. It is nontoxic to humans and breaks down in acid, yet standard water treatment cannot remove it, so suppliers need combined methods such as advanced oxidation. In the soil it carries signals. It attracts {{ref:soil-bio-085}}, which feed on these bacteria and spread their spores, and it repels the roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans.

soil-bio-114.title: Organic matter, the carbon left by living things
soil-bio-114.text: In 1828 Friedrich Wöhler made {{ref:soil-fert-021}} in a laboratory, and an old idea began to crack. That idea, vitalism, equated organic with living. Organic matter is the large pool of carbon-based compounds derived from the feces and remains of plants, animals and other organisms. Its basic structures come from cellulose, tannin and {{ref:soil-bio-116}}, plus the leaf coating in {{ref:soil-bio-233}}, with proteins, lipids and carbohydrates. After an organism dies, microbes and fungi break it down. The small products can recombine into larger, complex molecules. Its molecules range from 200 to 20,000 amu, and up to one-third of its carbon sits in stable rings that are hard to break. In soil, litter decayed beyond recognition counts as {{ref:soil-found-045}}. Organic matter carries nutrients, holds water and buffers solutions towards neutral pH. Most measurements capture only organic carbon, so they only approximate the amount of once-living matter.

soil-bio-138.title: Fibrous roots, the dense mat near the surface
soil-bio-138.text: A mature tree 30–50 m tall spreads its roots as far as its height or more, yet well over 95% of them lie in the top 50 cm. Within a few years, most trees switch from a taproot to this wide, shallow kind of network. A fibrous root system is a dense mat of many thin, similar-sized roots growing from the stem base, the opposite of a taproot system. It forms when the embryonic root dies back while the plant is young, leaving thin roots and no distinct taproot. In many species most of the mat is adventitious roots, roots that sprout from the stem base. Monocots, the flowering plants with one seed leaf, all have one, as do ferns; wheat and rice are typical. Fibrous roots bind soil, take up surface nutrients quickly and control erosion. Forage crops cover a whole field and anchor its top layer of soil. The root mats of meadow grasses may even help hold radioactive materials in place.

soil-bio-155.title: Growth-promoting bacteria, from seed coat to root
soil-bio-155.text: Joseph W. Kloepper first used the term plant growth-promoting rhizobacteria, or PGPR, in the late 1970s. They are soil bacteria that colonize plant roots after being inoculated onto seed, and they enhance plant growth. Directly, they fix nitrogen, make siderophores that chelate iron for the root, solubilize minerals such as phosphorus and make plant hormones. Indirectly, they limit the damage pathogens do to yield, through induced systemic resistance and antifungal compounds. To work they must survive on the seed, multiply in the spermosphere, attach to the root and colonize the root system. Failure to colonize often explains poor field results. Inoculants usually go on the seed coat so that enough bacteria establish, and those at the root tip were found most active. Most are Pseudomonadota and Bacillota, such as Pseudomonas putida and the lipoferum species of the genus in {{ref:soil-bio-237}}. As {{ref:soil-fert-048}} and biopesticides, they could raise yields and cut disease while reducing dependence on chemical fertilizers and pesticides.

soil-bio-187.title: Roots that move water from wet soil to dry
soil-bio-187.text: During a drought, a deep-rooted plant can draw up groundwater and release it into parched topsoil. Hydraulic redistribution is this passive movement of water by roots from moist soil to dry soil. It happens in plants rooted in both wet and dry soil. It is strongest in those with taproots reaching the water table and side roots near the surface. In drought, water rises up the taproot and seeps from the laterals into the dry surface soil. Under flooding, roots move water the other way. The xylem, the plant's water-conducting tissue, links taproot to laterals. Wet or dry soil around the laterals then sets up a pressure gradient, much like transpirational pull, the tug of water evaporating from leaves. It was once described as hydraulic lift: roots releasing water and nutrients into soil, mostly at night. Researchers now see two-way movement, helped by fungal networks described in {{ref:soil-bio-164}}. Hydraulic lift is regulated by the root endodermis, an inner sheath of root cells, and by stomata, the pores in leaves. Cavitation, air breaking the water column in the xylem, can stop it. By smoothing out differences in soil moisture, the process affects crop irrigation and helps seedlings establish. Scientists trace it with deuterium, a heavy form of hydrogen, and with sap flow and soil moisture measurements. Efforts are under way to add it to land-surface models.

soil-chem-081.title: One-to-one or two-to-one: how clay sheets stack
soil-chem-081.text: Clay mineralogists sort their subjects with two numbers. A 1:1 clay builds each layer from one tetrahedral and one octahedral sheet. A 2:1 clay places an octahedral sheet between two tetrahedral sheets. That difference decides how the layers hold together. 1:1 layers carry no charge and cling to each other by hydrogen bonds. 2:1 layers carry a net negative charge, so something positive must bind them. In some groups that is a scatter of cations; in others, a whole octahedral sheet. Four main groups result. The kaolin group, typified by {{ref:soil-chem-088}}, also holds dickite, {{ref:soil-chem-090}} and nacrite, all 1:1 clays like serpentine. The 2:1 groups are three. {{ref:soil-chem-091}} includes {{ref:soil-chem-093}}, nontronite, saponite and the clay of {{ref:soil-chem-152}}, and its layers are bound by cations. So are those of {{ref:soil-chem-094}}. {{ref:soil-chem-087}} is bound by octahedral sheets instead. Talc and {{ref:soil-chem-095}} are 2:1 clays too. Soil scientists usually give the same four groups for soils. Some clays break the pattern. {{ref:soil-chem-110}} and the clay of {{ref:soil-chem-167}} are 2:1 clays with long water channels inside their structure. Mixed-layer clays interleave two types, either randomly, coded R0, or in order. Perfectly ordered R1 mixes have their own names, such as rectorite and corrensite.

soil-chem-098.title: Imogolite, a clay built of nanotubes
soil-chem-098.text: Some clay comes as tubes about 2 nm across. Imogolite, Al2SiO3(OH)4, is an aluminium silicate clay mineral made of a network of these nanotubes. Each tube is 1 nm wide inside, with walls of gibbsite sheets and orthosilicate groups. It was first described in 1962 in Kumamoto prefecture, Japan, and named from imogo, a brownish-yellow soil derived from volcanic ash. It occurs in such soils with allophane, quartz, cristobalite, gibbsite, vermiculite and the iron mixture of {{ref:soil-chem-165}}. Where tephra is basic or the climate dry, allophane and imogolite develop, and {{ref:soil-class-119}} receive the Silandic qualifier.

soil-chem-112.title: Hematite, the blood-red oxide of old soils
soil-chem-112.text: Hematite takes its name from the Greek for blood. It is a common iron oxide mineral, Fe2O3, widely found in rocks and soils. Clay-sized hematite forms as a secondary mineral during soil weathering. With goethite and the other minerals of {{ref:soil-chem-163}}, it gives many tropical, ancient or highly weathered soils their red color. It grows from {{ref:soil-chem-111}}, a metastable precursor of both hematite and goethite. Red ochre is clay colored by 20% to 70% unhydrated hematite. Older ironstone crusts in {{ref:soil-class-137}} contain more hematite and boehmite than plinthite does.

soil-chem-117.title: Standard electrode potential: ranking the electron takers
soil-chem-117.text: Fluorine scores +2.866 V, zinc ions −0.763 V, and hydrogen ions exactly zero. These are standard electrode potentials: the equilibrium voltage of a half-reaction under standard conditions, measured against the reference of {{ref:soil-chem-179}}. Also called a reduction potential, the value measures how strongly an oxidizing agent tends to be reduced. Hydrogen sits at zero by definition. Stronger oxidants score positive, weaker ones negative. The value is given in volts or millivolts. A cell's potential is the cathode potential minus the anode potential.

soil-class-001.title: Putting the world's soils in order
soil-class-001.text: Long before modern science, priests in Egypt were sorting soils. Inscriptions at the temple of Horus at Edfu record a soil classification used to choose temple sites, and ancient Greek scholars devised several more. Soil classification is the systematic grouping of soils by their distinguishing characteristics and by criteria that guide how they are used. Modern systems group soils by measurable traits such as texture, structure, mineral composition and the way the soil formed. Soil science, engineering and environmental management all classify soils, to judge their properties and decide on suitable land use. Soil can be treated as a material, as geotechnical engineers do when judging foundations and building material, or as a resource. The major modern systems include {{ref:soil-class-006}}, the {{ref:soil-class-016}} and engineering systems that judge stability and performance, met in {{ref:soil-class-002}}. Standard systems matter because they let soils be compared across regions and uses. Knowledge of where soils occur has also grown dramatically. The project of {{ref:soil-meth-017}} now maps soils worldwide at 1.00–0.25 km resolution, built from soil profiles and environmental data. Still, the subject keeps moving. The structure of systems, the definitions of classes and their use in the field all continue to change.

soil-class-111.title: Paleopedology, reading the soils of lost worlds
soil-class-111.text: Around 1795, observers in Scotland saw cliff soils that seemed to be remains of a former land surface. Paleopedology, the study of soils of past geological eras, began there. Its methods combine soil science and paleontology. Hilgard related soils to climate in the United States in 1892, and by the 1920s Glinka had found Russian soils that were relics of warmer climates. Fossil soils lie under sediment or volcanic ash, or where younger soil has eroded away, as in South Dakota, home of the ground in {{ref:soil-water-269}}. Buried soils lose their vegetation and organic matter. Yet the shape and size of root traces still reveal what grew on them. X-ray diffraction, developed since the 1960s, now lets paleosols be placed in the 12 soil orders. Many Precambrian soils fit no modern order. These 'green clays' are colored by unoxidized minerals that formed before free oxygen.

soil-env-023.title: Bioremediation: putting microbes to work on pollution
soil-env-023.text: After the 2010 Gulf of Mexico oil spill, bacteria and archaea that could live on petroleum helped restore the coast. They used the oil as a source of both carbon and energy. That is bioremediation: using organisms, living or dead, to remove pollutants from soil, water, air and other media. The usual workers are bacteria, microalgae, fungi or plants. The method exploits their natural ability to absorb, accumulate and degrade pollutants, building on the living world of {{ref:soil-bio-011}}. It aims to be more sustainable, cheaper and more scalable than physical and chemical treatment. Most bioremediation is inadvertent, done by native organisms without help. Research focuses on speeding it up by inoculating sites with organisms or supplying nutrients. Chemically, most of these processes are redox reactions. An added electron acceptor, usually oxygen, oxidizes pollutants such as hydrocarbons, making them more soluble in water and easier to degrade. In the end, the breakdown described in {{ref:soil-env-231}} turns hydrocarbons into carbon dioxide and water. Alternatively, an added electron donor reduces pollutants such as nitrate, perchlorate and chlorinated solvents. Toxic metals mark the hard limit. They cannot be biodegraded, only oxidized or reduced, so bioremediation offers few solutions for them. Techniques work in situ, at the site itself, or ex situ, on excavated material. They range from pumping air into soil to heaping dug soil in aerated piles, and plants can join in, as {{ref:soil-env-037}} shows. The main challenge is rate. The processes are slow.

soil-env-034.title: Fungi that soak up metals, and even gold
soil-env-034.text: Filtering electronic waste through fungi has recovered 80% of its gold. In fungi, the process in {{ref:soil-env-219}} is the capture of metals: they bind them on their cell surfaces and concentrate them in their fruiting bodies for later removal. Pleurotus, Aspergillus and Trichoderma remove lead, cadmium, nickel, chromium, mercury, arsenic, copper and zinc, on land and in water. Metals enter the mycelium passively, and strains from long-polluted sites tolerate them best. Some mushrooms become bioindicators: the edible shaggy ink cap signals mercury well, but can then be toxic to eat. Even dead fungal cell walls can filter heavy metals and radionuclides from industrial effluents.

soil-env-215.title: Arctic methane and a feedback still taking shape
soil-env-215.text: Arctic-Boreal lands release about 48.7 Tg of methane a year, a 2024 assessment found, and marine sources add about 4.9 Tg. The gas comes mainly from thawing permafrost, melting sea ice, the breakdown of clathrates and the melting Greenland ice sheet. Clathrates are icy solids that trap gas inside, and they hold about 20 Gt of permafrost-associated methane. Permafrost itself holds almost twice as much carbon as the atmosphere. The emissions form a positive climate feedback. Thaw exposes organic material to methanogenesis, and methane is a powerful greenhouse gas. Thermokarst lakes are frequent sources, and at least half the methane made in them reaches the atmosphere. Dating by the method in {{ref:soil-hist-120}} suggests 0.2 to 2.5 Pg of permafrost carbon was released as methane and CO2 over the last 60 years. The future pace is debated, as {{ref:soil-env-159}} showed. A 2015 review found anaerobic thaw sites, those without oxygen, emitted 75-85% less in total than aerobic ones. A 2018 seven-year incubation found methane production matched CO2 once methanogenic microbes became established. For now, no evidence ties the Arctic to the methane rise since about 2018, which points instead to tropical wetlands. Its role, though, will very likely grow.

soil-fert-012.title: Granules or solutions: the two forms of fertilizer
soil-fert-012.text: About 90% of fertilizers reach crops as solids: granules, powders or prills. Urea, potassium chloride and the compound in {{ref:soil-fert-206}} are the most common. Liquid fertilizers are water-based solutions of ammonia, urea or the salt in {{ref:soil-fert-071}}. Liquids act faster and cover more evenly, while granules are cheaper to ship, store and apply. Dissolving fertilizer in the water piped to crops is the subject of {{ref:soil-fert-208}}. It places nutrients where the water goes and allows small doses, reducing fertilizer use and leaching. Growers use it mostly on high-value crops such as vegetables, turf, fruit trees and ornamentals.

soil-fert-067.title: Organic mulch and the hidden cost of straw and sawdust
soil-fert-067.text: A layer of straw looks harmless, yet it can briefly slow the plants beneath it. Organic mulch is made of plant or animal residues, such as leaves, straw, bark, wood chips or manure, and it decays over time. Straw, peat, sawdust and wood products are rich in carbon but poor in nitrogen, so the microbes decomposing them draw nitrogen from the soil. Such mulches can also mat into a barrier to water and air. Growers use fully composted material to avoid the plant damage described in {{ref:soil-env-222}} and seed-free material to keep out weeds. Peat moss lowers surface pH, which suits acid-loving plants, but once wetted and dried it can form a crust that water cannot soak into.

soil-fert-119.title: Denitrifying bacteria, a crowd from many branches
soil-fert-119.text: Over 50 genera and 125 species can denitrify, an estimated 10–15% of the bacteria in water, soil and sediment. Denitrifying bacteria are a diverse group, drawn from many phyla, that carry out {{ref:soil-fert-108}}. They use nitrate and nitrite in place of oxygen as the final electron acceptor. Most are facultative aerobic heterotrophs, organisms that feed on organic carbon, such as species of Pseudomonas, Alcaligenes and Bacillus. They switch to nitrate when oxygen runs out. Four enzymes act in turn: nitrate reductase, nitrite reductase, nitric oxide reductase and finally the enzyme of {{ref:soil-fert-225}}, which yields nitrogen gas. Their electrons come from organic carbon, or from hydrogen, reduced iron or sulfur. In one soil, the drilosphere, the soil shaped by earthworms, held 16 per cent of them. By sending nitrogen back to the atmosphere they lower soil fertility, releasing nitric oxide and the greenhouse gas nitrous oxide on the way. Wastewater plants put them to work, feeding them organic carbon in an oxygen-free basin so nitrate bubbles off as nitrogen gas.

soil-fert-163.title: Reading a hungry plant: signs of nutrient deficiency
soil-fert-163.text: Crops can starve without looking starved. Nutrient deficiency covers the effects of too little of an essential nutrient, from slightly slower growth to stunting, deformity, discoloration and death. Clear-cut symptoms are rare, because most deficiencies are multiple and moderate. Nitrogen is most often the nutrient in shortest supply. Its lack brings stunted, slow growth and yellowing leaves, a sign covered in {{ref:soil-fert-228}}, sometimes with purple stems and leaf undersides from the pigment anthocyanin. A shortage of phosphorus, the subject of {{ref:soil-fert-232}}, is hard to diagnose, though leaves may turn intensely green, reddish or purple. Calcium shortage, covered in {{ref:soil-fert-227}}, weakens root systems and causes blossom end rot in tomatoes, peppers and watermelons, bitter pit in apples and black heart in celery. A shortage of potassium, covered in {{ref:soil-fert-233}}, starts in older tissues, with necrosis or yellowing between the veins, wilting, more disease and greater frost and heat damage. Iron, manganese and copper deficiencies show on new growth, molybdenum on older growth, zinc on old and new leaves, and boron on terminal buds. That yellowing is not always about nutrients. Solarization looks similar, but unlike deficiency it causes no early leaf drop.

soil-form-002.title: The soil profile, a record read from the top down
soil-form-002.text: Going down a soil profile means going back in time. Like layers of sediment, its horizons record past events. A soil profile is a vertical face of soil showing its horizons, layers roughly parallel to the surface. Formally, it is one face of the three-dimensional block described in {{ref:soil-form-003}}. Soil scientists expose a profile by digging a pit or extracting a core with a hand or hydraulic push tube or an auger. Mature profiles typically have three basic master horizons, A, B and C, but no profile has all the major horizons. Some soils, such as those of the {{ref:soil-class-094}} order, have only one horizon or none. Young soils on mine waste, moraines, volcanic cones, dunes or alluvial terraces are examples. Wind or running water can strip the upper horizons and bury them downslope, a natural process that {{ref:soil-agri-095}} aggravates. Major earthworks or regular deep plowing can leave a soil almost without distinct horizons. The horizons also hold clues to the past. Pollen, {{ref:soil-bio-195}} and plant remains can reveal changes in climate or land use, and large pieces of charcoal allow dating by the method in {{ref:soil-hist-120}}.

soil-form-023.title: Subsoil, where the rain drops its cargo
soil-form-023.text: Rain does more than wet the ground. It carries weathering products such as clay and the minerals of {{ref:soil-chem-163}} downward, dissolved or as fine suspended particles, and most of them settle in the subsoil. Subsoil is the layer beneath {{ref:soil-form-021}}, a mix of sand, silt and clay with much less soil organic matter. With so little of it, the subsoil's color comes mainly from those iron minerals. Physical, chemical and biological activity cluster its particles into a definite arrangement, and that sets it apart from the barely altered substratum below. It is not sterile, but it holds few soil organisms compared with the rich layer above. Most soil mapping systems give it the letter B, with a substratum lettered C beneath; {{ref:soil-form-010}} and {{ref:soil-form-011}} return to both. Human activity has mixed topsoil and subsoil in many environments. Builders have used clay-rich subsoil for millennia, as adobe, cob, rammed earth and wattle and daub.

soil-form-032.title: Illuviation: where washed-down material comes to rest
soil-form-032.text: Everything water carries out of an upper layer has to stop somewhere. Illuviation is that stopping: the deposition in a lower layer of material, called illuvium, washed down by rainwater from a layer above. It is the matching half of eluviation. Illuvium includes soil organic matter, silicate clay and the iron and aluminum compounds of {{ref:soil-chem-162}}. These collect in subsoil horizons lettered B, the zones of illuviation, described in {{ref:soil-form-010}}. The movement is basically vertical, unlike alluviation, the sideways transfer by running water. It works in two ways. In mechanical illuviation, a drier horizon draws water from percolating suspensions by capillarity, the pull of water into fine pores. Fine coatings are left along the channels, the subject of {{ref:soil-found-068}}. In chemical illuviation, dissolved constituents carried down by percolating water are deposited where the chemistry of the soil changes, especially its pH and its {{ref:soil-chem-123}}. Clay skins are called argillans, and horizons with enough washed-in clay are the ones named in {{ref:soil-class-045}}. In medium-textured soils, clay is often washed down the profile and gathers in the subsoil.

soil-form-050.title: Leaching: how water strips a soil from the top down
soil-form-050.text: Water soaking down through a soil does not travel empty. Leaching is the removal of soluble materials from one zone of a soil to another by water moving through the profile. It differs from eluviation, which moves tiny mineral and organic particles, the subject of {{ref:soil-chem-154}}, rather than dissolved material. Both tend to strip the topsoil and enrich the subsoil, in a horizon called the zone of illuviation. Climate sets the pace directly. Leaching is most intense in warm, humid regions where the soil does not freeze. The red tropical soil described in {{ref:soil-form-065}} develops under high temperatures and heavy rainfall, and intensive leaching leaves it less fertile than other soils. Its signature shows in the profile. In one brownish leached soil, {{ref:soil-class-049}}, water washes mobile chemicals out of the A horizon. Iron and aluminum oxides, the subject of {{ref:soil-form-085}}, gather in the B horizon and color it rusty orange-brown. The Canadian system for naming soils marks strongly leached layers as light gray Ae horizons. In Solonetzic soils, progressive leaching moves salts and sodium downward. The process can also defeat reclamation: intensive leaching has left reclaimed {{ref:soil-chem-030}} infertile.

soil-form-078.title: Soil memory: a record written over and over
soil-form-078.text: Dokuchaev called soil 'a mirror of the landscape'. In 1953 Nikiforoff echoed him with a new term, soil memory: the idea that soil keeps a record of past natural changes, environmental conditions and human activity. Soils store that record like a page written over and over, with newer features overprinting older ones. This is pedomemory; layered sediments instead store lithomemory, like a book in datable order. The idea is used to study climate change, land-use history and archaeological evidence. Persistent genetic traces in cultivated soils, the subject of {{ref:soil-hist-090}}, are read as a 'memory effect'. Yet most soils have developed under more than one set of conditions, so the record is partial and 'censored'. Equifinality, different paths leading to the same result, complicates reading it, and the concept serves as an exploratory tool.

soil-form-090.title: Glacial till, the unsorted load a glacier drops
soil-form-090.text: A boulder in a field may have come from an outcrop hundreds of kilometres away. Glacial till is unsorted sediment eroded and carried by a glacier and deposited directly from the ice. No liquid water carried it, so it is unsorted and unlayered. It is mostly clay, silt and sand with scattered pebbles, cobbles and boulders, often in a bimodal size distribution with two peaks. Its stones are often faceted, scratched or polished by glacial abrasion. Basal till, laid beneath the glacier, is typically very compact and slow to take in water. Ablation till, dropped as the ice melts, is less compacted. Till builds the terminal, lateral, medial and ground forms described in {{ref:soil-form-150}}, and the ridges called drumlins and flutes. Archibald Geikie first applied the term to primary glacial deposits in 1863. The older name, boulder clay, has fallen out of favor. Melting glaciers rework till into outwash and into lake or sea deposits such as varves.

soil-form-103.title: Superficial deposits, the young loose cover
soil-form-103.text: Most of the loose ground people walk on is geologically young. Superficial deposits are recent, mostly unconsolidated deposits, typically of Quaternary age, less than 2.6 million years old. They include stream channel and floodplain deposits, beach sands, talus gravels, raised beaches and {{ref:soil-class-065}}. Glacier-laid material belongs too, as {{ref:soil-form-149}} and {{ref:soil-form-150}} describe. Most are gravel, sand, silt and clay. Onshore they form relatively thin, often discontinuous patches. Geological surveys keep databases of their properties. Farmers and foresters use them to judge erosion, growing conditions and the risk of nutrients washing out.

soil-found-001.title: Soil horizons, the layers that record a soil's life
soil-found-001.text: Cut down through a soil and you usually cross a series of bands. Each band is a horizon: a layer roughly parallel to the surface whose physical, chemical and biological traits differ from those above and below. Horizons are made by soil-forming processes. Layers those processes have not touched are simply called layers. Given time, an undifferentiated soil evolves a profile of two or more horizons. They differ greatly in thickness and generally lack sharp boundaries. Most are recognized by color and texture, described outright or relative to their neighbors, as coarser, sandier or darker. No profile has every major horizon, and some soils, such as soils described in {{ref:soil-class-094}}, have one horizon or none at all. Horizons are also fragile. Erosion can strip the upper ones and bury others downslope, and tillage, tree growth and major earthworks disturb or erase them. Going down a profile goes back in time. Pollen, {{ref:soil-bio-195}} and plant remains record past environmental change, and charcoal allows a horizon to be dated by the method in {{ref:soil-hist-120}}. Most classification systems define soil types by horizons, either as whole sequences, as in the German system, or as selected diagnostic horizons. A shorthand of letters and numbers labels each one, recording color, texture, structure, consistency, roots, pH, voids, boundaries and nodules.

soil-found-024.title: Buffering: why some soils shrug off acid
soil-found-024.text: Add the same acid to two soils, and one barely budges while the other's pH plunges. The difference is buffering capacity, a soil's resistance to a change in pH when acid or basic material is added. It works through {{ref:soil-chem-047}} and neutralization, and carbonates also regulate pH. Different buffer systems take over at different pH, from calcium carbonate to iron. Pure sand has almost no buffering ability. Soils rich in fine mineral or organic particles, the subject of {{ref:soil-chem-154}}, buffer strongly. Within one kind of soil, buffering rises with {{ref:soil-chem-046}}. So clay- and humus-rich soils need more lime for the same change in pH. The reason is stored acidity. Lime must neutralize the acid cations held on these particles, not just the free acid in solution, or the stored cations restore the original pH. The lime needed depends on how finely it is ground and on buffering capacity. Once the particles are saturated with hydronium, the buffer is spent, and further acid drives pH lower.

soil-found-034.title: Carbonate minerals and the geologist's acid test
soil-found-034.text: Field geologists carry dilute hydrochloric acid for a quick test. All carbonates react with acid, so a drop tells them apart from other minerals. Carbonate minerals are those whose main anionic group is carbonate, [CO3]2−. The chief ones are aragonite, dolomite and the mineral in {{ref:soil-found-118}}. That last one, CaCO3, is the most common, and the main constituent of limestone and marble. Dolomite is the double carbonate CaMg(CO3)2. Carbonates usually form as biogenic or chemical sediments in marine settings. Weathering by dissolved carbon dioxide, sometimes called carbonation, can also produce secondary carbonate minerals.

soil-found-041.title: How rain and time turn feldspar into clay
soil-found-041.text: Granite carries the makings of clay. One of its minerals, a kind of {{ref:soil-form-141}} described in {{ref:soil-form-143}}, weathers to {{ref:soil-chem-088}} and silicic acid, releasing potassium ions. Clay formation is the making of {{ref:soil-chem-079}}, most commonly by long chemical weathering of silicate-bearing rocks, and their gathering into deposits. The work is done largely by acid hydrolysis. Weak carbonic acid in rainwater, or acid released by plant roots, breaks the bonds between aluminum and oxygen. Other metal ions and silica come loose, the silica as a gel of orthosilicic acid. Source rock and climate decide the product. Feldspar-rich rock gives kaolin under warm, acid weathering, and {{ref:soil-chem-094}} under alkaline conditions. Under alkaline conditions, the rock of {{ref:soil-form-135}} yields {{ref:soil-chem-091}}. Intense weathering of other such minerals produces an aluminum hydroxide. Hydrothermal activity can also make them locally. Then the clay may travel. Primary clays stay where they formed, as residual soil deposits. Secondary clays are carried off by flowing water and laid down elsewhere, often in large lakes or marine basins.

soil-found-057.title: Salt weathering: crystals that pry rock apart
soil-found-057.text: Salt can split stone. In salt weathering, also called haloclasty, salty water seeps into cracks and evaporates, leaving salt crystals that grow there. Like {{ref:soil-phys-154}}, the grains draw in more dissolved salt through tiny gaps. They grow into lenses that press hard on the surrounding rock. Sodium and magnesium salts work best. Salt weathering happens wherever evaporation concentrates salts, so it is most common in arid climates and along coasts. In the rocks of {{ref:soil-form-136}}, weathering of {{ref:soil-chem-134}} to iron(II) sulfate and gypsum can grow salt lenses too.

soil-found-062.title: Mineral hydration, water's first grip on a crystal
soil-found-062.text: Before water can take a crystal apart, it has to attach to it. In mineral hydration, water molecules, or H+ and OH− ions, attach rigidly to the atoms of a mineral. The minerals of {{ref:soil-chem-163}} turning into iron hydroxides, and anhydrite hydrating to gypsum, are examples. Bulk hydration matters less than dissolution, hydrolysis and oxidation. But hydration of the crystal surface is the crucial first step in hydrolysis. Water at a fresh surface splits into H+ and OH−. Protons then replace the positive ions at the surface, freeing them. Loosened bonds release silicic acid and aluminum hydroxides. In the mineral of {{ref:soil-form-141}}, this starts at defects on the crystal surface, in a layer only a few atoms thick.

soil-found-089.title: Grassland and desert soils, shaped by drought
soil-found-089.text: Drought writes itself into a soil. Grassland and desert soils form where rain and snow equal or fall short of the water lost to evaporation and plants. Little water and few organic acids percolate downward. So the washing out of dissolved substances slows, along with chemical breakdown of minerals and soil development itself. Evaporation builds up calcium in the upper profile, where it clumps clay and dissolved organic acids together. Lower down, calcium settles out as a hard layer of the mineral in {{ref:soil-found-118}}. In deserts a layer of gypsum and halite may lie beneath it. Where rain and washing out increase, the clay-richest layer sits deeper.

soil-phys-003.title: Peds: the natural building blocks of soil
soil-phys-003.text: A lump of earth gets a different name depending on who made it. When soil-forming processes build it, it is a ped: a natural aggregate of soil particles, set apart from its neighbors by pores or voids. When cultivation makes it, it is merely a clod. The word, a contraction of pedolith, is used mostly for visible units larger than 1 mm seen in the field. Peds form as sand, silt and clay clump into aggregates, and aggregates clump into larger units. Coatings of carbonates, clay, silica, humus and the minerals of {{ref:soil-chem-163}} glue them into fairly stable secondary structures. Some soils are structureless, while others have simple units or compound units built of smaller ones. The gaps between peds are one way large pores, or {{ref:soil-water-189}}, form, alongside roots, cracks and soil animals. Peds are best described when soil is dry or slightly moist, because wet peds blur together.

soil-phys-062.title: Particle density: the weight of the grains alone
soil-phys-062.text: Leave out the pores and soil grains come to a density of typically 2.60 to 2.75 g/cm3. That is particle density: the density of the solid particles alone, not counting the voids between them. It usually stays the same for a given soil. It is lower in soils rich in organic matter and higher in soils rich in the minerals of {{ref:soil-chem-163}}. Because {{ref:soil-phys-060}} includes the pores, it is always less than particle density, and it varies widely with biological activity and management while particle density does not. Together the two give {{ref:soil-phys-063}}. A mean particle density of about 2.65 g/cm3 is used for silica sediments and 2.70 g/cm3 for carbonate ones.

soil-phys-092.title: Soil mechanics: how a mix of grains, water and air behaves
soil-phys-092.text: A dam, a pipeline and a house foundation all rest on the same question: how will the soil behave? Soil mechanics is the branch of soil physics and applied mechanics that answers it. Unlike fluid or solid mechanics, it deals with a mixture: fluids, usually air and water, among particles of clay, silt, sand and gravel, plus organic solids. With rock mechanics it underpins engineering geology and the field traced in {{ref:soil-phys-167}}. It analyses how structures built on, made of or buried in soil deform, and how fluids flow inside them, from foundations and retaining walls to dams and pipelines. Agricultural, coastal and geophysical engineering and hydrology use its principles too. One idea runs through it. A load pressing down on soil is shared between the pore fluid and the particles. Neither gas nor liquid resists shear, though, so resistance to sliding comes from friction and interlocking of the grains. Standard classification tests miss part of the story. They use dried, sieved and remoulded samples, so the soil's structure and its pattern of pore sizes and fluids are lost.

soil-phys-110.title: Consolidation: the slow squeeze that sinks buildings
soil-phys-110.text: Picture a spring inside a water-filled container with a hole in its lid. Press the lid and at first the water resists. Then it drains out through the hole, and the spring shortens and takes over the load. The spring is the soil skeleton. The process is soil consolidation. It is the gradual change in a soil's volume under a change in pressure, as water is slowly squeezed out of or drawn into its pores. When saturated soil is loaded, the water, far stiffer in volume than the skeleton, first carries the load as excess pore water pressure. As it seeps away, the grains take the load and the soil shrinks. Saturated clays consolidate very slowly, because water passes through them with extreme difficulty. Coarse soils drain readily and settle at once instead. Clays settle under external loads, under their own weight or that of overlying soil, and when groundwater pumping raises the effective stress on them. The effects show most where a building sits on soft, poorly permeable soil such as marine clay, which can settle a great deal over many years. In the narrow sense the term means this delayed, drainage-driven response. In the broad sense it covers any pressure-driven volume change, including compaction, sinking land, heave and swelling. Karl von Terzaghi, the 'father of soil mechanics', defined it as any loss of water from a saturated soil without air taking its place. Engineers measure it with the test in {{ref:soil-phys-170}}, loading a thin disc of soil in steps and recording its thickness over time.

soil-phys-127.title: Sand boils, where buried water breaks the surface
soil-phys-127.text: In a flood, water pushed through a levee can well up on the dry side as if it were boiling: a sand boil. Turbulent flow at the seep starts the underground erosion of {{ref:soil-water-289}}, which can quickly fail the embankment, so crews stack rings of sandbags to slow it. Earthquakes that liquefy saturated sediment make sand boils too, sometimes building a cone called a sand blow. The 1811–1812 New Madrid earthquakes left the largest known, 'The Beach' near Hayti, Missouri, 2.3 kilometres long. Geologists map sand blows as strong evidence of past earthquakes.

soil-phys-154.title: Ice lenses, the hidden engine of frost heave
soil-phys-154.text: Most of the lift in frost heave comes from ice growing in hidden layers underground. An ice lens is a body of ice that forms where moisture moving through soil or rock collects in one zone, usually parallel to the surface. Ice first gathers in small pores or cracks. It keeps collecting there, wedging the soil or rock apart. Lenses grow several centimeters to several decimeters deep, and their growth is the dominant cause of soil displacement in frost heaving. They draw water from groundwater below the freezing line, through fine soils with capillary pores. The water can travel because water in fine pores stays liquid below the normal freezing point, the Gibbs–Thomson effect. The same process, the subject of {{ref:soil-phys-179}}, splits rock more effectively than the freeze-thaw expansion proposed by older texts. Arctic tundra favors deep lenses, because permafrost keeps the ground frozen at depth and stops meltwater draining away.

soil-phys-185.title: Seasonal frost, ground that freezes and thaws each year
soil-phys-185.text: Each winter some ground freezes and each spring it thaws. This seasonal frost is one of three kinds of frozen ground classed by how long they stay frozen, beside permafrost and the frost of {{ref:soil-env-149}}. Its repeated freezing and thawing pushes larger stones toward the surface, building patterned ground such as polygons. Cryogenic earth hummocks, formed by granular convection, appear here as well as in permafrost. Builders take note: rigid retaining-wall footings must sit below the seasonal frost depth, the reach of the {{ref:soil-phys-158}}.

soil-phys-203.title: Groundwater: the water held in the pores of the Earth
soil-phys-203.text: About 30 percent of the world's readily available fresh water is groundwater. It is water held beneath the Earth's surface in the pore spaces of soil and rock and in rock fractures. In the technical sense it includes soil moisture, the frozen ground of {{ref:soil-env-129}} and immobile water in tight bedrock, not only water flowing in shallow {{ref:soil-phys-201}}. It enters naturally as infiltration that percolates down to the water table, and leaves through springs and seepage to the oceans. It is a long-term store of the water cycle, with residence times from days to millennia. In the Great Artesian Basin it travels about 1 meter per year and can be more than 1 million years old. About 70% of extracted groundwater is used in agriculture, and that use carries risks. Where salty water evapotranspires, salts are left behind. Poor drainage in irrigation districts can raise water tables to the surface, causing soil salinity and waterlogging. Pollution, often from improper waste disposal on land, spreads in plumes and is harder to clean up than surface water pollution.

soil-phys-217.title: ET0: the water use of an imaginary lawn
soil-phys-217.text: Crop water use is measured against an imaginary patch of grass. Reference evapotranspiration, written ET0, is the water a standard, well-watered grass surface would lose under the current temperature, humidity, wind and solar radiation. FAO 56 defines that grass precisely as a hypothetical crop 0.12 m tall, actively growing and adequately watered. It has a surface resistance of 70 s m-1 and a reflectivity of 0.23, the quantity treated in {{ref:soil-phys-177}}. The FAO derived its Penman–Monteith equation to model it. Multiplying ET0 by {{ref:soil-phys-218}} gives the evapotranspiration of unstressed plants, ET = Kc × ET0. A stress coefficient then gives actual crop use. Weather-based irrigation controllers calculate it.

soil-water-025.title: Rills, the first scratches of an erosion problem
soil-water-025.text: The first sign that a field is losing soil is often a set of tiny channels. Rills are shallow channels, no more than a few centimeters deep, cut into soil by flowing surface water, and rill erosion is the erosion that happens in them. Smaller incised channels are microrills. Larger ones are the subject of {{ref:soil-water-027}}. Hillslope runoff cuts rills into unprotected soil, as on farmland left bare, after deforestation or during construction. Rills are easy to see when first cut, so they often give the first warning of an erosion problem. Tractors help start them. They compact the soil so that water runs over it, and their wheel tracks channel the water into rills. Flow in a rill is typically a few centimeters deep or less, so its hydraulics differ greatly from flow in streams and rivers. It is still strong. Rill flow may carry nearly ten times as much as the interrill areas between rills. In moderate rain it can move rock fragments up to 9 cm across. Without conservation measures, rills can grow into those larger channels or, in semi-arid regions, into the bare, carved ground of {{ref:soil-water-269}}. Under good management, contour tilling repairs them.

soil-water-040.title: Computer models of soil on the move
soil-water-040.text: Tillage erosion models are computer models that simulate how cultivation moves soil along a hillslope or across a field. The simplest are one-dimensional hillslope models such as TEP and TillERI. They use slope length, gradient and the erosivity of the operation to give erosion rates and risk. WaTEM calculates both water and tillage erosion on a grid of ground heights, as in {{ref:soil-agri-164}}. It treats the soil shifted by each pass as diffusion in the steepest-slope direction. Field-scale models such as SORET and TillEM add the direction of cultivation, moving soil both parallel and perpendicular to it.

soil-water-067.title: Trees on a slope: anchor or burden
soil-water-067.text: The same large trees can steady a slope or help bring it down, depending on where they stand. At the toe of a slope prone to rotational failure, they could raise its factor of safety by 10%. Planted at the top, they could lower it by 10%. The link between slopes and plants runs both ways, shaped by soil type, rainfall regime, plant species, the direction a slope faces and its steepness. Plants act in four main ways: wind throw, removal of water, their added mass, called surcharge, and reinforcement by roots. Wind throw topples a tree and exposes its root plate, a risk for single trees more than for sheltered stands. Mass matters only for large trees: one 30–50m tall may load a slope with roughly 100–150 kN/m2. Felling big trees at the toe removes both their drying effect and their load. In clay soils the resulting suction can then draw in water and soften the soil.

soil-water-156.title: Saturated flow pushes water; unsaturated flow pulls it
soil-water-156.text: Unsaturated flow moves water at most about 2.5 cm a day. So roots cannot wait for water to come to them; they keep dying back and growing toward moister soil. Water moves through soil in two modes. Between 0 and 33 kPa suction, up to {{ref:soil-water-177}}, gravity and differences in water pressure push water away from where it was applied. This is saturated flow. At higher suctions, water's adhesion to soil solids sets up a suction gradient. It pulls water from wetter to drier soil and from macropores to micropores: unsaturated flow. As soil dries, its connected wet pathways shrink, so the conductivity described in {{ref:soil-phys-225}} falls in a very non-linear way. Six factors control infiltration and movement: texture, structure, {{ref:soil-bio-114}}, depth to impervious layers such as hardpans or bedrock, water already present and how warm the soil is. Warm soils take in water faster. Frozen soils, including permanently frozen ground, may not absorb it at all, depending on how they froze. {{ref:soil-water-238}} gives the rate of change of moisture in unsaturated soil. Lewis Richardson first published it in 1922, and software such as Hydrus solves it numerically.

soil-water-209.title: Hydropedology, where soil science meets hydrology
soil-water-209.text: Hydrology likes to pair with the Earth's other spheres, as hydroclimatology, ecohydrology and the field in {{ref:soil-phys-208}} show. Hydropedology is the emerging field that joins soil science and hydrology. It studies the interface between the pedosphere and the hydrosphere, the planet's water. Soil hydrology and hydropedology are both listed among the areas of practice of soil science. The biomantle shows what the field studies. Loosened by {{ref:soil-bio-047}}, it speeds downward drainage through biopores and carries throughflow downslope above dense subsoil horizons.

soil-water-246.title: Potential evapotranspiration: how much water the air demands
soil-water-246.text: Summer, clear skies, wind and nearness to the equator all raise the air's demand for water. Potential evapotranspiration is the water a crop, soil or ecosystem would evaporate and transpire if water were not limited. It reflects the energy and wind available to move water vapor, the demand side of {{ref:soil-water-161}}. Actual evapotranspiration equals it when water is ample and can never exceed it. The reference rate, ET0, the subject of {{ref:soil-phys-217}}, is calculated for a short-grass surface, most widely with the FAO-recommended equation in {{ref:soil-phys-215}}. A crop factor, described in {{ref:soil-phys-218}}, and a stress coefficient then convert it into a crop's actual evapotranspiration.
